title: Brains, light and chips: practical steps to low‑energy computing
label: 4 November 2026 · Low‑energy computing
summary: Experts explained two complementary routes to much lower‑energy computing: neuromorphic systems that process information like a brain (event‑driven, memory and compute together) and silicon photonics that use light to move and process data with far less power. Both are already real but face the same practical barriers: scaling from lab demos to reliable, mid‑volume manufacturing, limited access to major foundries, and insufficient patient capital. The witnesses asked for focused UK action—national pilot lines, clearer Government engagement with global foundries, procurement as an early customer, and £100m‑scale funding to accelerate deployment.

glossary.definition: Hardware and systems designed to work like biological brains: memory and compute together, event‑driven processing, and low energy use.
A kind of neural network that processes information as discrete 'spikes' over time, enabling event‑based, real‑time learning.
A vision sensor that only reports changes (events) in the scene, producing much less data than full frame cameras.
A factory that mass‑manufactures semiconductor chips from designs provided by other companies.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world’s largest contract chipmaker (foundry).

chapters.title: What neuromorphic computing does and why it matters
chapters.takeaway: Neuromorphic systems mimic brain principles—co‑located memory and compute, event‑driven spikes—to cut energy and speed up decision‑making at the edge.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We want practical industry views on low‑energy computing. Tanya, please explain the analogue neuromorphic technology you use.

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: Analogue Insight designs chips for companies. We focus on analogue and mixed‑signal work that natively implements spiking neural networks—so devices behave more like brain circuits than digital emulations.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What do you mean by 'spiking'?

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: Spiking neural networks use timing: units emit events or spikes only when needed. That makes them event‑based, training and adapting in real time, and hugely more energy efficient for certain tasks.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: Neuromorphic systems take lessons from brains, not always copying them exactly. For example, brain‑like devices can be paired with photonics to exploit very high data rates while keeping energy low.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: A useful distinction: signals (environmental changes), the data we digitise, and the information we care about. The brain produces much less data by only reporting important events—event cameras for vision are a clear example.

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: That matters for data centres: currently energy is often spent moving and storing data. Neuromorphic devices co‑locate memory and compute, reducing movement and cutting energy dramatically.

chapters.title: UK strengths, barriers and practical asks
chapters.takeaway: The UK has strong research, materials IP and prototypes (SpiNNaker, memristor work), but lacks access to major foundries, patient capital and end‑to‑end scale‑up—so witnesses ask for coordination, pilot facilities and government help engaging foundries.

turns.speaker: Maya Ellis
turns.text: How is the political and market reception? Where are the barriers—funding, appetite or something else?

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: We have the IP and materials research, but to commercialise we need foundries to accept new processes. Big foundries (TSMC, GlobalFoundries) control recipes. UK teams can’t easily get those doors opened.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: It often takes about $100m to move a lab technology to commercial silicon. The UK lacks sufficient patient capital and a risk culture like Silicon Valley. Government procurement as a first customer would materially help.

turns.speaker: Daniel Zeichner
turns.text: Do we have industrial capacity in the UK to manufacture at scale?

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: No country except Taiwan covers every piece. The UK can own parts of the chain: design, niche manufacturing (Pragmatic, Paragraf), photonics clusters and silicon carbide in Wales—but mass production will need international partnerships.

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: We already have SpiNNaker and small foundries that could make chips for edge applications. The problem is lack of coordination and an end‑to‑end plan to move lab IP into fabs.

turns.speaker: Kit Malthouse
turns.text: Why don’t big foundries pick up UK IP if it’s that good?

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: We met TSMC in 2025. They asked who in the UK would lead such engagement. Universities alone don’t have the authority; Government needs to present a clear partner and route to scale.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: The UK Semiconductor Centre could be that coordinating body, and extended programmes—sustained five‑year funding, centres for doctoral training, national testbeds—would help build an ecosystem.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: DSIT pledged £20m to neuromorphic computing to 2030—will that deliver sovereign capability?

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: No. It can seed activity but is far short of the sums and scale needed to deliver sovereign manufacturing capability.

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: Agreed. Going lab to fab realistically needs much more capital and Government help to unlock foundry engagement.

chapters.title: Silicon photonics: light as the path to lower energy
chapters.takeaway: Silicon photonics uses light on tiny chips to move and process data with far lower energy; it’s already being deployed but needs mid‑scale pilot manufacturing to bridge lab demos to mass production.

turns.speaker: Dr Josh Silverstone
turns.text: Photonics is the technology of light. At Hartley we build photonic neuromorphic devices to do AI inference extremely fast—valuable where time matters: finance, defence, robotics, fusion control and satellite comms.

turns.speaker: Professor Callum Littlejohns
turns.text: Silicon photonics integrates light devices onto chips. It can transmit vast data volumes at much lower energy than electronics, and is already being used in data‑centre links; its role is growing as AI demands explode.

turns.speaker: Freddie van Mierlo
turns.text: How ready is the tech?

turns.speaker: Professor Callum Littlejohns
turns.text: It’s being deployed now. Big commercial deals and investments are happening. The bottleneck is scale‑up: proving you can manufacture many reliable wafers and packages, then moving to mass foundries.

turns.speaker: Tom Collins
turns.text: Is a UK pilot line realistic?

turns.speaker: Professor Callum Littlejohns
turns.text: Yes. A national pilot line would produce tens of thousands of wafers a year (we model 10–20k) and prove designs at volume so companies can pitch to global foundries. It’s a mid‑scale, shared facility.

turns.speaker: Dr Josh Silverstone
turns.text: GlobalFoundries and other mid‑sized fabs can make these designs; their existing capacity far exceeds what a startup needs. But without a UK pilot capability, companies struggle to scale and are vulnerable to being deprioritised abroad.

chapters.title: Policy choices, timescales and risks
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses want Government to coordinate, back pilot facilities, use procurement as bridge, and enable stronger engagement with foundries; accelerating timelines to 2–3 years would need ~£100m of patient capital.

turns.speaker: Martin Wrigley
turns.text: What prevents big firms like Nvidia from buying UK IP and taking it offshore?

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Kenyon
turns.text: Nothing in practice stops acquisitions. The country’s interest is to anchor companies and talent—shared infrastructure helps do that so purchases are more likely to leave R&D and jobs here.

turns.speaker: Dr Tanya Mangoma
turns.text: Start‑ups that secure IP and commercial customers fast—examples like Fractile—are best protected. But Government can help by creating a clear route to scale and by using diplomatic weight with foundries.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What concrete asks should we recommend?

turns.speaker: Professor Callum Littlejohns
turns.text: Build a national pilot line (shared, fee‑accessed), fund testbeds and doctoral training, include neuromorphic and photonics in AI hardware strategy, and use procurement to be an early customer where appropriate.

turns.speaker: Dr Josh Silverstone
turns.text: If the goal is to compress the timeline to 2–3 years for some high‑impact products, expect to mobilise an extra ~£100m of capital for companies and infrastructure; at present many are working on ~£10m rounds.

turns.speaker: Tom Collins
turns.text: If the pilot line is built quickly, when might it deliver economic impact?

turns.speaker: Professor Callum Littlejohns
turns.text: A facility built in three to four years could start creating meaningful GVA by the early‑to‑mid 2030s; our modelling shows sizeable economic returns if scaled properly.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. The Committee will consider these asks: co‑ordination, pilot facilities, procurement pull and larger, patient capital to translate strong UK research into sovereign capability where sensible.
